awd_titl_txt: STTR Phase I: Development of Seed Applied Bacterial Consortium for Soybean to Increase Yield, Nitrogen Fixation, Disease Resistance, and After-Harvest Soil Nitrogen Content
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project will include substantial economic and commercial benefits for organic soybean growers, consumers, and the United States. This project will develop a combination of bacteria applied via seed coating to reduce soybean disease outbreaks, reduce soybean fertilizer needs, and increase soybean yield. Currently, the United States remains heavily reliant on imported organic soybeans, with over 80% sourced from countries such as Turkey, India, and Argentina. This project aims to support American soybean farmers in transitioning to organic production by providing them with a solution that can replace pesticide and fertilizer applications that are used in conventional agriculture. The successful execution of this project would thereby reduce dependence on imports and strengthen domestic agricultural markets. By increasing local organic soybean supply, this effort has the potential to enhance economic resilience and contribute to the national agricultural sector. Beyond economic and commercial benefits, this project also supports societal benefits like property health concerns from nitrogen fertilizer run-off. In the United States, improper nitrogen management contributes significantly to algal blooms and fish die offs in waterways, thus solutions such as this project can reduce nitrogen fertilizer use thus reducing nitrogen run-off.

The proposed project seeks to address challenges faced by organic soybean growers related to plant pathogens and nitrogen availability. This research aims to develop a microbial seed coating that enhances organic soybean production by simultaneously reducing pathogen-associated yield loss and improving nitrogen fixation. The overarching goal is to develop a bacterial consortium that promotes soybean disease resistance, nitrogen fixation, yield, and soil nitrogen availability. The proposed project will achieve these objectives through a set of field and greenhouse trials designed to evaluate the impact of the seed-applied bacterial consortium on soybean growth and productivity. Specifically, these trials will assess disease resistance to damping-off pathogens, including Fusarium, Pythium, and Phytophthora, through disease incidence scores and stand counts. Additionally, soybean tissue nitrogen concentration and final yield will be measured to determine consortium effects on nitrogen fixation and productivity. Post-harvest soil samples will be analyzed to quantify residual nitrogen availability. Rhizosphere samples will be collected throughout the growing season and examined to identify microbial strains associated with improved plant and soil characteristics, facilitating iterative optimization of the consortium. These findings will contribute to the development of an effective microbial inoculant for organic soybean production, enhancing both disease management and nitrogen efficiency.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcomes Report

Soybean is one of the most economically important crops in the United States, but early-season seedling diseases, including those caused by the fungi such as Fusarium can reduce stand establishment and yield. Farmers commonly protect seeds with synthetic fungicide coatings to mitigate these losses. Biological seed treatments consisting of beneficial soil microbes could offer an alternative that also supports plant health and nutrient uptake thereby reducing the need for synthetic fungicides. However, relatively few microbial-based seed coatings have been rigorously tested against industry-standard products under real field conditions.

In this Phase I STTR project, Earnest Agriculture partnered with the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign to evaluate two of the company's microbial consortium seed coatings in field trials. The trials were expanded beyond the original plan to include three fields and 180 experimental plots. Half of the plots were inoculated with F. graminearum to create disease pressure, and three nitrogen fertilizer levels were included to test performance under different soil fertility conditions. The microbial products were compared with an untreated control and with two commercial synthetic fungicide seed treatments. Throughout the season, the team measured stand counts, disease incidence, root nodulation, plant biomass, seed protein content, and final yield. The team also used PacBio long-read DNA sequencing to track how the treatments changed the bacterial and fungal communities in the soybean rhizosphere.

Both microbial consortia produced higher soybean yields than the synthetic fungicide treatments, with yield advantages ranging from 2.75% to 7.8% greater than these treatments. Plots treated with the microbial products also had 26% to 28% more established plants than plots treated with the synthetic fungicides on average. Under disease pressure, the microbial products reduced disease incidence by 10.5% to13.5% relative to the untreated control, a level of protection statistically comparable to the synthetic fungicides. The products did not change seed protein content, which suggests that nitrogen was not limiting at these sites. Microbiome sequencing showed that the microbial seed treatments significantly altered the bacterial community around young soybean roots, while fungal communities responded more to nitrogen and pathogen treatments than to seed treatment.

Intellectual Merit: This project produced field-scale evidence on how multi-species microbial seed treatments perform against conventional fungicide seed treatments under controlled disease pressure and varying soil fertility. Combining agronomic measurements with long-read amplicon sequencing improved the team's ability to distinguish product microbes from native soil microbes and to show when, during the season, seed treatments influence root-associated communities. The project also identified open questions, such as how soil nitrogen status and product storage affect performance, which will guide future research.

Broader Impacts: Biological seed treatments that perform as well as synthetic chemistry could give growers new tools for managing seedling disease, support more sustainable farming practices, and diversify crop protection options. The results provide practical, comparative data that farmers, agricultural retailers, and agronomists need to evaluate biological products. The project strengthened a collaboration between a small agricultural biotechnology company and a land-grant university, and it expanded the company's research capacity. The team plans to publish the findings in a peer-reviewed journal. The next phase of work will test product consistency across diverse soils, shelf stability during storage, and large-scale manufacturing, which are key steps toward bringing an affordable biological seed treatment to market.
